description: How a fresh community gets into the federation network: one public route that hands out peers to dial. Every running community is a bootstrap node, because every running community already serves HTTP.

routes.name: peer.bootstrap

fields.name: self
fields.description: The answering community's own node. Always present, so one URL yields at least one dialable peer even from a community that knows nobody yet.

fields.name: peerId
fields.description: The libp2p peer id, derived from the community key pair. See contracts/test-vectors — the derivation is contracted because the two implementations must agree on it.

fields.name: addresses
fields.description: Multiaddrs the node listens on, most reachable first. TCP and QUIC entries for the same node are separate addresses, not one address with two transports.

fields.name: peers
fields.description: A sample of nodes this community has seen recently and believes reachable now, at most DHT_BOOTSTRAP_PEERS_MAX of them. A sample, not the top of a list: a joining node needs a few *different* entry points, because Kademlia fans out from wherever it starts. Two calls a minute apart may legitimately return different peers. May be empty.

fields.name: lastSeenAt
fields.description: When this community last had contact with that node. A caller uses it to order its dialing, not to decide trust.

notes: Public on purpose. Bootstrapping happens before any handshake exists, so a route that required authentication could not be the way in.

What this returns is a hint, not a trust decision. Whoever answers could hand out a poisoned list. These peers are somewhere to start dialing; who a community *is* is settled by the federation handshake against communities.public_key. An implementation that treats a bootstrap answer as authority has moved the trust boundary to whoever typed a URL into a config file.

No request parameters and a fixed bound. A bootstrap endpoint that takes a limit, a filter or a cursor is an enumeration endpoint, and this one deliberately is not: it hands out enough to join the network and no more. Sampling rather than ordering makes that structural — nobody can walk the network by calling it repeatedly.

Current in the DHT sense, not complete. What belongs here is what was seen recently and is believed reachable now — not the federated_communities table, which knows who ever announced. An answer full of nodes that announced once years ago is a slow failure rather than a fast one.

The default bootstrap URL is DHT_BOOTSTRAP_DEFAULT_URL. That makes the ordinary case safe without making it a protocol guarantee: the two mechanisms that hold when an operator points somewhere else are the per-peer handshake, and later the signed variant below.
Legacy has no counterpart. libp2p, unlike hyperswarm, comes with no public network to join, and this route is gradido2's answer to that — see fast-servers/dht-node/Architecture.md, Bootstrap.

open.question: What does the signed variant look like on the wire?
open.detail: Running the federation handshake with the bootstrap community first, and having it sign what it returns, turns an anonymous hint into an attributable statement — it removes the impostor at a hijacked URL. It does not make the named peers trustworthy; that stays the per-peer handshake's job. No signature field is contracted yet, on purpose: fixing a shape before the handshake-first flow is designed would fix the wrong one.
open.why_it_matters: Verifying a signature needs the signer's public key, so a bootstrap entry becomes a URL *and* a key rather than a URL. For DHT_BOOTSTRAP_DEFAULT_URL that key can ship as a default; for any other it is one more thing an operator must configure correctly. Which is why the unsigned route is what lets a community join at all, and the signed one is hardening on top rather than a replacement.

open.question: How recent is 'seen recently'?
open.detail: The sample needs a freshness bound, and both implementations must use the same one or the two hand out different notions of current.
open.why_it_matters: A disagreement here is not visible in any single response — it shows up as one path bootstrapping reliably and the other not.
open.status: unanswered — belongs in const.json once there is a node to measure against
